content_html:
Neurons - Decay, Renewal, and Regeneration

Most mature neurons are long-lived and do not divide, yet their molecules and synapses turn over continuously. Adult hippocampal neurogenesis in humans remains debated; multiple studies support persistence with age, while others report it is minimal or undetectable. In the peripheral nervous system (PNS), axons can regenerate with help from Schwann cells; in the central nervous system (CNS), regeneration is strongly limited by inhibitory cues and low intrinsic growth capacity.

  • Most mature neurons are post-mitotic and long-lived, sustained by proteostasis and glial support.
  • Protein turnover is continuous, with a subset of exceptionally long-lived proteins potentially contributing to age-related vulnerability.
  • Adult hippocampal neurogenesis in humans remains contested; multiple studies support persistence into old age, others report near-zero levels.
  • Peripheral nerves can regenerate axons with Schwann-cell–mediated repair; CNS regeneration is limited by inhibitory cues and intrinsic growth programs.

Lifespan vs renewal: neurons persist, molecules turn over; neurogenesis is an exception (debated in humans); regeneration differs in PNS vs CNS.
